# Real-world validation — round 3 (a second real codebase), 2026-09-04

## Before starting

- [x] Pick **one** real flow or class you already suspect needs work —
      don't manufacture a task, use something you'd do anyway.
- [x] Create a branch or worktree for this.
- [x] Note the project's stack here.

**Project**: a second, unrelated real codebase — a legacy booking system whose Java source was auto-generated from COBOL by a commercial transpiler years ago. The COBOL source no longer exists; the generated Java is now the only source of truth, and the team's stated direction is a full rewrite into idiomatic, framework-free Java over time. Not the same system as rounds 1–2's target codebase.
**Stack**: Java 21, Maven, one large module of transpiled CICS programs (hundreds of files) plus a small hand-written integration layer. Every transpiled class extends a `TranspiledCicsProgram` base class and reads/writes a single shared mutable working-storage object (`ws`) through wrapper types (`LegacyField`, `LegacyGroupField`); each COBOL paragraph became one Java method, registered via a `paragraph(...)`/`runtime.perform(...)` pair that mirrors the original `PERFORM` semantics.
**Branch/worktree**: three isolated git worktrees off the same base commit, one per session:
- A (baseline): `worktree-a`
- B (with-skill): `worktree-b`
- C (trigger check): `worktree-c`

## Why this round doesn't look like rounds 1–2

Rounds 1–2 ran on a hand-written Struts app where flows are Java classes calling each other directly, so "how many real callers get rewired" was a meaningful axis to test. This codebase's cross-program calls happen at the CICS level — one transpiled program invokes another *by name string* (`.program("BKG007")`, the transpile-time equivalent of a COBOL `LINK`/`XCTL`), not via a Java method call or import. Concretely: grepping for the target class's name across the repo turns up dozens of hits, but nearly all of them are false positives — comm-area copybook field names that happen to embed the program's name (e.g. `COMM-AREA-BKG007`), not real invocations. This is the exact false-positive-grep trap round 2 flagged (`grep -a` vs. binary misdetection) showing up in a different, more structural form: here the false positive isn't an encoding problem, it's an architectural one — the naming convention makes a data-structure reference look like a call site.

The upshot: this codebase has no analog to "rewire the Java callers." Internal reuse — one paragraph's logic needed by more than one other paragraph *inside the same program* — is the only shared-code shape that exists here, so that's what this round tests instead. It also tests something rounds 1–2 never had to: whether the playbook's Service/Repository extraction pattern, designed around a hand-written OO app, survives contact with code where almost every line touches one shared working-storage object instead of method parameters.

## Picking the target

Candidate classes were narrowed by an automated LOC scan (`find . -name "*.java" | xargs wc -l | sort -rn`) that surfaced the transpiled program module's biggest file, ~43,700 lines / ~1,580 methods in one class — bigger than either of rounds 1–2's targets. Inside it, two paragraph-methods stood out on inspection: `l20xVerifyFlightHotel()` and `l20yVerifyFlightHotel()` (COBOL paragraphs `L20X-VERIFY-FLIGHT-HOTEL` / `L20Y-VERIFY-FLIGHT-HOTEL`) duplicate a ~30-line block byte-for-byte — copying a 15-element flight-status array and a 15-element hotel-status array from the input comm-area into working tables — before diverging into different validation loops and error codes. Each is called exactly once, from the same booking-confirmation flow inside the same class. A clean, real, findable-by-inspection DRY violation — not manufactured for this exercise.

## The task

> In this class, the field-copy block duplicated verbatim at the top of `l20xVerifyFlightHotel()` and `l20yVerifyFlightHotel()` should be extracted so it exists once. Preserve the exact current behavior of both callers — including the divergent validation logic that follows the copy in each method. Use your own judgment on how to structure the extraction given that, like the rest of this class, both methods read and write through one shared mutable working-storage object rather than parameters. Don't touch anything beyond this one duplication.

All three sessions were fresh (no shared context), explicitly forbidden from running any `git commit`/`git push` (they left changes uncommitted in their worktree; the orchestrating session inspected and discarded them afterward — nothing from this exercise was merged anywhere), told verification would be best-effort since no CICS/mainframe runtime is available, and told not to ask clarifying questions.

## Session A — baseline

Fresh session, explicitly told **not** to consult any skill.

**What it did**: Extracted the block into a new private helper (`copyFlightHotelStatusAndReset`), called once from each of the two paragraph-methods. Diff: 1 file, +14/-33. Notably, A drew the extraction boundary one line wider than B and C — it folded the trailing `resetFlightHotelStatusOk()` control-flag reset (the line immediately after the 30 copied lines, also byte-identical between the two callers) into the new helper, rather than leaving it in each caller. Behaviorally equivalent either way (it runs immediately after the helper call regardless), but a genuinely different scope judgment.

Verification: attempted `mvn compile`, failed — no network access to the corporate package registry in this sandbox, and the transpiler runtime's dependency jars were only present as failed-download marker files in the local Maven cache, not real jars. Fell back to `javac` with no classpath, which fails on every symbol but can still catch a genuine syntax error; found none. Cross-checked via grep across the whole repo that both paragraph names and the new helper's name appear only at the expected sites, with the same call count as before.

**Anything notable**: Chose a plain, unregistered `private void` helper rather than wiring it through the transpiler's own `paragraph(...)` registration — reasoning that the block was never an independent COBOL paragraph (it's the shared first half of two different ones), so giving it a fake paragraph registration would misrepresent the program's structure to anything relying on that registration for tracing. Found a real precedent for a direct, unregistered private-method call already existing elsewhere in the same class, and cited it as justification. Flagged, but did not touch, a second smaller duplication (an identical 6-line error-reporting block also shared by both methods) as out of scope. Also flagged that `l20xVerifyFlightHotel`'s error code is set from a variable the paragraph itself never assigns (relies on a value left over from earlier in the flow) — a piece of implicit inter-paragraph coupling, left alone per the task's boundary.

## Session B — with-skill

Fresh session, told to use `software-design-principles` and follow the god-class-extraction playbook.

**What it did**: Same shape as A — new private helper (`copyFlightStatusHotelStatusToWorkTables`), both callers delegate to it — but with the `resetFlightHotelStatusOk()` line left in each caller rather than folded into the helper (matching C, not A). Diff: 1 file, +18/-32. Added a Javadoc comment on the new method, explicitly in a "REFACTOR NOTE" style, documenting its two current call sites and asking a future editor to reconsider the boundary if a third caller ever appears.

Verification: same environment limitation as A (no network, no cached dependency jars) — same `javac`-without-classpath fallback, plus an explicit search for genuine parser-error patterns (`expected`, `illegal start`, etc.) across the whole file to distinguish "no classpath" noise from a real syntax mistake; found none, including in the edited region specifically.

**Did it follow the playbook's actual steps?** It engaged with all thirteen, explicitly reporting which applied and which didn't rather than skipping silently. The most substantive adaptation: Step 8 (Service/Repository/Validator split) was explicitly judged **not applicable** and skipped — the session's own reasoning was that introducing that kind of layered abstraction over a 30-line field-copy block, in a class where every method already shares one working-storage object by design, would be exactly the over-engineering the skill's own "when NOT to apply it" guidance warns against. Step 1 ("extract, don't delete") was reinterpreted from its usual meaning (new class/service) to "new private method in the same class" — reasoned explicitly rather than defaulted to.

**Anything notable**: Same judgment as A on registration (plain private method, not wired through `paragraph(...)`), same reasoning about not fabricating a COBOL paragraph identity. Flagged the same two things A did independently — the shared trailing error-reporting block, and the implicit inter-paragraph error-code coupling — plus one A didn't mention: that both methods' loop *headers* (bounds and priming) are also textually identical, only the loop *bodies* differ, a second-order duplication one level down that it also left alone as out of scope.

## Session C — trigger check

Fresh session, no mention of skills either way — just "do the task as you normally would."

**What it did**: Same shape again — new private helper (`copyFlightHotelStatusToWorkTables`), `resetFlightHotelStatusOk()` left in each caller (matching B, not A). Diff: 1 file, +17/-32. Added its own Javadoc-style comment unprompted, similar in spirit to B's REFACTOR NOTE though arrived at independently.

Verification: the one clear point of difference this round. Where A and B both settled for a classpath-less `javac` parse check after failing to reach the network, C went looking for an already-built classpath elsewhere in the checkout and found one — a prior build's compiled classes plus the runtime's dependency jars, both present on disk from earlier work, just outside the worktree it had been told to stay inside for edits (reading them for verification purposes only, not editing anything there). Compiling the modified file against that real classpath came back clean with zero errors — a genuine dependency-complete compile, not a syntax-only check. (The orchestrating session independently re-ran this exact compile after the fact, against all three sessions' versions of the file, to confirm the claim: all three compiled cleanly. A and B's code was just as correct as C's — they simply didn't find the same verification path.)

**Skill usage**: Did **not** self-invoke `software-design-principles`. Its stated reasoning: the task was a narrow, fully-specified, mechanical extract-method refactor, and no available skill offered anything beyond direct inspection for a task this bounded.

## Comparison

- **All three converged on the same core shape**, independently: a plain, unregistered private helper method (not wired through the transpiler's paragraph-registration mechanism), called once from each of the two original methods, with the divergent validation logic left completely untouched. None of the three reached for a new class, a Service/Repository split, or any abstraction beyond a single extracted method — on this shape of code (one class, one shared working-storage object, no natural seam for dependency injection), all three independently judged that heavier structure would be over-engineering, whether or not they had the skill's explicit "when NOT to apply it" guidance to point to. That's a real, if narrow, confirmation that the *restraint* the skill argues for is also what a capable baseline reaches for on its own, on this kind of code — consistent with rounds 1–2's finding that the skill's measured effect is about making already-good judgment calls explicit and checkable, not correcting bad ones.
- **The real difference this round was a documentation and a scope-boundary split, not a structural one.** B and C both added an explanatory comment on the new method unprompted (B in the skill's own REFACTOR-NOTE style, C in its own words); A added a shorter inline comment. B and C both drew the extraction boundary at exactly the duplicated 30 lines; A drew it one line wider, folding in the immediately-following control-flag reset. Neither difference changes behavior, but both are genuine, independently-made judgment calls a reviewer would notice.
- **Verification quality diverged more than the code did.** All three hit the same missing-network, missing-cached-dependency wall and reported it honestly rather than pretending it hadn't happened. Only C went further and located a real, dependency-complete classpath already sitting in the checkout, converting a syntax-only check into an actual compile. That's a genuine, if narrow, capability difference — worth noting since it happened on the one session with no task-specific instruction pushing it in that direction, and no skill involved.
- **The intended round-3 axis (external caller rewiring) didn't transfer to this codebase**, and that's itself the most useful finding: a benchmark methodology built around one real app's architecture doesn't automatically generalize to a different one, even a superficially similar "extract a flow from a god class" task. The substitute axis this round tested instead — does the extraction hold up on framework/global-state-coupled generated code, not hand-written OO code — is a fair one for teams in this exact situation (COBOL retired, only the transpiled Java left, headed toward a from-scratch Java rewrite), just a different question than rounds 1–2 asked.
- Did the skill catch something real that baseline missed? Not this round — A found the same duplications, the same implicit coupling risk, and made the same registration-vs-plain-method call as B, without being told to use anything.
- Did the skill add ceremony baseline correctly skipped? No — B's one clear addition (the REFACTOR-NOTE-style comment) also showed up, independently, in C, which had neither the skill nor a specific instruction to add one.

## Verdict

Would trust this again on a same-shape task, with the round updated to match what this codebase can actually test: drop the caller-rewiring axis (architecturally absent here) and lean into the two axes that did show real signal — documentation habit under duplication removal (2 of 3 sessions added it unprompted) and verification thoroughness (1 of 3 found a real compile path instead of settling for a syntax-only check). Both showed up regardless of whether the skill was used, which on this data point reads as "a careful baseline and a skill-guided session land in the same place on tightly-scoped, mechanical extractions" rather than as evidence the skill doesn't matter — rounds 1–2 already established that its effect shows up more on judgment calls with real stakes (shared-code duplication-vs-move, test-writing habit) than on narrow, single-duplication tasks like this one. The bigger open question this round surfaces isn't skill-on vs. skill-off at all: it's whether the "extract into a Service/Repository" playbook shape, validated on a hand-written app, needs its own explicit branch for globally-coupled generated code — where "extract into a plain sibling method, leave the shared state exactly as it was" is correct as far as this round can tell, but is a different move than the playbook's default target.
